lesson.title: Flipping the Tap: The RL High-Pass Filter
lesson.summary: Taking the output of the same series RL circuit across the inductor instead of the resistor turns the low-pass response into a high-pass one, blocking low frequencies and passing high ones.
lesson.body:
Just as the RC high-pass filter is nothing more than the RC low-pass filter with the output tapped from the other component, the RL high-pass filter is the RL low-pass filter with the output taken across the inductor instead of the resistor. Same two parts, same series connection, different measurement point, opposite frequency behavior.

At DC and low frequency, the inductor's reactance XL = 2*pi*f*L is small, so very little voltage develops across it, and the output stays near zero. As frequency rises, XL grows, more of the input voltage appears across the inductor, and the output rises toward the full input amplitude at high frequency. Low frequencies are blocked, high frequencies pass through nearly unattenuated, which is exactly the definition of a high-pass filter.

The cutoff frequency is found the same way as before, at the point where R equals XL, giving the identical formula fc = R / (2*pi*L). It is worth pausing on that: the RL low-pass and RL high-pass filters built from the same R and L values share exactly the same cutoff frequency. The only difference is which side of the divider you read, and therefore which side of that cutoff gets passed and which gets blocked.

Try R = 500 ohms and L = 20 millihenries (0.02 H). Then fc = 500 / (2*pi*0.02) = 500 / 0.1257, which is about 3978.9 Hz. Now apply an 8 V amplitude signal at f = 1000 Hz, below that cutoff, and see how much survives. The angular frequency is w = 2*pi*1000 = 6283.2 rad/s, so wL = 6283.2 x 0.02 = 125.66. The high-pass magnitude ratio for this circuit is wL / sqrt(R^2 + (wL)^2) = 125.66 / sqrt(500^2 + 125.66^2) = 125.66 / sqrt(250,000 + 15,791) = 125.66 / sqrt(265,791). The square root of 265,791 is about 515.6, so the ratio is 125.66 / 515.6, about 0.244. Multiplying by the 8 V input gives roughly 1.95 V at the output. Because 1000 Hz is less than one decade below the 3978.9 Hz cutoff (the ratio is about 0.25, not a full order of magnitude), the attenuation is noticeable but not yet as severe as the idealized 20 dB per decade asymptote would suggest far from cutoff, which is a useful reminder that the simple rolloff rule is only accurate once you are safely away from the cutoff region itself.

As with its low-pass sibling, the RL high-pass filter is less common in practice than the RC high-pass filter, mainly because inductors are bulkier and less ideal than capacitors at the frequencies most everyday circuits care about. But the underlying reasoning, reactance rising with frequency, output tapped across the element whose reactance dominates at the frequencies you want to pass, carries forward directly into the RLC band-pass filter next, which combines both an inductor and a capacitor in the same circuit.
